Gutzon Borglum. The American sculptor famous for monumental public works carved directly into stone and granite. His masterpiece, Mount Rushmore, remains one of the world's largest sculpture projects—a feat of engineering, artistic vision, and nationalist ambition that defined American public sculpture in the twentieth century.

Borglum designed and directed the carving of Mount Rushmore from 1927 to 1941, embedding the faces of Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, and Theodore Roosevelt into a South Dakota mountain. He pioneered large-scale stone carving using pneumatic tools and explosives, enabling sculpture at monumental scales that had previously been impossible. Earlier in his career, he sculpted the Mares of Diomedes in 1904, a dramatic marble group of rearing horses showing classical influence.

Borglum conceived Mount Rushmore as a nationalist symbol—American presidents carved in permanent stone as an assertion of permanence and power. He died before Mount Rushmore was fully finished, and his son Lincoln Borglum completed the work. He also designed the unfinished Crazy Horse Memorial in South Dakota, an even larger horse-and-rider carving that remains under construction. Mount Rushmore stands as his defining work and an American icon of engineering marvel.
